Prevention: Use certified seeds from reliable sources such as
KALRO Mwea, NIA Use resistant varieties that can tolerate the disease pressure such as
Plant early to avoid late season high disease pressure.
Do not use previous seasons seed as the pathogen is seed borne
Weed fields to eliminate grass weeds that could serve as host plants
Use proper seed rate: broad casting, 100kg/ha; transplanting, 50kg/ha.
Avoid high humidity levels that favor the disease
Avoid excessive use of nitrogenous fertilisers.
Use fertiliser at recommended rates of (NPK 17:17:17, 125 kg/ha) at basal and at both tillering and panicle initiation stages
Rotate with non-host plants like cassava to break the disease cycle
Uproot volunteer rice that could harbour the pathogen
Monitoring: Spindle-shaped lesions or spots with grey centers surrounded by brown margin on leaves
Look for lesions on the leaf collar culm, culm and neck nodes, and on the panicles.
They enlarge and coalesce killing the entire leaf
Look for infection at the nodes.
Culms break at the infected node
Look for infection at the junction of the leaf blade and sheath resulting in brown collar rot symptoms
Grain sterility is observed as “white heads” and few seeds are produced
Look for grey-brown lesions on panicle branches and stems of florets
Take action when 2-5 plants are infected
Direct Control: Uproot infected plants and destroy by burning
Apply silica (Calcium silicate) to reduce soil acidity which favors the pathogen
Use antagonistic biocontrol agents such as
P®, Rootgard®) for seed dressing at recommended rates
Improve silicon in the soil by applying 1000
Restrictions: When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label
Do not use chemicals with the same mode of action year after year as this can lead to resistance
Always consult the most recent list of registered pesticides (PCPB)
Rodazim (20ml/20L of water) (Chariot 20ml/20L of water), at maximum tillering and at panicle
